principles.text: Be useful, not personal: write about the reader's problem and how to solve it, not about your own story.
AI raises the average, not everyone. Taste, judgment and experience are the edge it can't supply.
Never one-shot AI output: generate many variations, then use your taste to pick and patch together the best.
Use AI for what you're already good at. If you're bad at the thing, you can't judge the output.
Grow first, monetize later: give tested, step-by-step content away free and the people who value it will pay.

sampleQA.question: How do I start growing on LinkedIn from zero?

answer.text: Pick one problem to solve and only that one. If you can't state your mission in one sentence, it's too broad.
Stay on one platform and write for one persona until you reach millions of views before expanding.
Test formats and angles for 30 days, then repeat your best five for the next month and drop the losers.
Posting is about a third of the game; the rest is commenting, DMs and networking.

sampleQA.question: Why is my AI output so generic, and how do I fix it?

answer.text: It's usually missing context, not a bad model: you didn't give your tone, audience or rules.
Write a brief, not a wish: a role, examples to imitate, and expectations for format, length and tone (R-E-X).
State your goal and success criteria, then ask the AI to ask you clarifying questions before it starts.
Treat the first draft as about 60% there, steer with short redirects, and write the final 5% yourself.

sampleQA.question: How do I stop hitting Claude's usage limits?

answer.text: Claude re-reads the whole conversation on every message, so long chats get expensive fast.
Edit your original message instead of sending corrections, and batch several tasks into one prompt.
Plan in Chat, build in Cowork, and save Opus with extended thinking for deep work.
Start a new chat after roughly 30-50 turns, when it starts to get worse.
